analysis.one_liner: Charges large cargo ships a pollution fee at U.S. ports and spends the money on cleaner shipping.
analysis.headline: The bill went no further than a Senate committee: referred on introduction in June 2023, it never received a hearing markup or vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a price on pollution from large cargo ships that off-load at U.S. ports: $150 per metric ton of carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions from the fuel they burn on voyages ending at a U.S. port, plus fees for nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, and fine particulate matter in U.S. waters, with the rate rising each year with inflation plus 5 points [S2] [S3]. It reaches ships that unload U.S.-bound cargo at foreign ports, credits fees a foreign country already charges, and sunsets if the International Maritime Organization adopts an equal or larger global fee [S2] [S3]. The money would be spent on decarbonizing the U.S. merchant fleet, low-carbon maritime fuel research, battery-electric harbor craft and ferries, clean ports, air monitoring within a mile of port boundaries, and training at maritime academies [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: People living near ports, who breathe ship exhaust today, and everyone affected by shipping's climate emissions, which the bill's own findings say account for nearly 3 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions [S3]. Domestic ship owners, harbor craft and ferry operators, maritime fuel producers, and maritime academies would gain access to funded programs, and port communities would gain fenceline air monitoring [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a $150-per-metric-ton fee on lifecycle carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions from fuel burned on covered voyages ending at U.S. ports, tripled for fuel burned in polar regions, and adjusts upward annually by inflation plus 5 percentage points [S3].

Adds per-pound fees on nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, and fine particulate matter from fuel burned in U.S. waters, targeting the pollutants that the bill's findings tie to poor air quality and worse health outcomes in neighborhoods around ports [S3].

Routes 53 percent of the collected revenue into programs for the public and the domestic fleet: replacing or retrofitting Jones Act vessels (25 percent), Energy Department research on low-carbon fuels and technologies (25 percent), harbor craft electrification (10 percent), ferry electrification (10 percent), workforce training at maritime academies (5 percent), fenceline air monitoring within a mile of ports (3 percent), plus funding for the clean ports program, port infrastructure, ocean security, and marine debris programs [S3].

Covers ships that off-load U.S.-bound cargo at foreign ports by charging importers a prorated fee, and requires importers to pay before U.S. Customs releases the cargo, preventing shippers from dodging the fee by stopping just short of a U.S. port [S3].

Credits vessels for pollution fees already paid to a country of origin, and the whole fee ends if the International Maritime Organization enforces a global fee at least as large, aiming to push international standards rather than simply tax U.S. arrivals [S3].

analysis.who_pays: International ocean shipping lines and the importers of goods they carry would pay the fees, and shipping costs like these are generally passed on to buyers, so prices on imported goods would likely rise. Nearly everything American consumers buy from overseas arrives by ship.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ocean shippers, importers, and ultimately consumers

drawbacks.text: The fee would raise the cost of moving goods by sea, a cost shippers and importers generally pass along to consumers, so Americans would likely pay more for imported goods from toys to appliances [S2] [S3].

The rate is set high from day one and escalates automatically by inflation plus 5 percentage points each year, with no congressional review, so the price shock to trade would grow over time regardless of how the industry adapted [S3].

A single-country fee applies only to voyages ending at U.S. ports and requires extensive voyage-by-voyage reporting from ship operators and importers, creating compliance costs and a risk that trade partners treat it as a unilateral levy even though it credits foreign fees and sunsets against a global equivalent [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and climate case is real: shipping is a large and growing source of carbon dioxide and port neighborhoods bear the brunt of the pollutants the bill fees. The costs fall on shipping lines and importers but would partly reach consumers through prices on imported goods, and the automatic escalator plus the multi-agency enforcement scheme make it a heavy-handed instrument. A designed-by-committee version with a lower starting rate and a built-in review would be easier to defend; as written, the bill asks trade to absorb a steep and growing charge that a fair vote would have forced Congress to debate.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's Environment and Public Works Committee never took it up after referral, so it sat there until the 118th Congress ended and the bill expired.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on June 8, 2023 with Senators Alex Padilla and Peter Welch as original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day [S1] [S3] [S5].
Four Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill, all from one party, and no Republican did [S4].

The committee took no further action: the complete action history shows nothing after the June 8, 2023 referral, and the bill died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: International ocean shipping lines and importers are better off because the bill died, since they avoided a per-ton emissions fee on U.S.-bound voyages. Port-neighborhood residents and domestic clean-shipping programs gained nothing, because the funded programs never existed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ocean shipping lines that avoided the fee

industries.note: The bill charges these operators per ton of emissions on every voyage ending at a U.S. port, plus pollutant fees in U.S. waters, with docking bans for nonpayment. Their cost would largely be passed through to consumers of imported goods.

industries.industry: Importers and retailers of overseas goods
industries.note: Importers must report, pay, and prove payment before Customs releases U.S.-bound cargo off-loaded abroad, adding cost to the supply chain for consumer goods.

industries.industry: Domestic Jones Act ship owners and shipbuilders
industries.note: A quarter of the fee revenue funds grants, rebates, and loans to replace or retrofit U.S.-flagged vessels with battery or low-carbon propulsion, with priority for projects cutting emissions and pollution in overburdened areas.
A quarter of the revenue funds competitive Energy Department grants to produce, transport, blend, or store low-carbon maritime fuels, creating a domestic market the fee itself would demand.

industries.industry: Ports, harbor craft, and ferry operators
industries.note: The bill funds electrification of harbor craft and ferries, clean ports programs, port infrastructure, and fenceline air monitoring in communities within a mile of port boundaries.
Five percent of revenue funds workforce training at maritime academies for zero-emission port equipment and battery or low-carbon vessels.
